Thermodynamic-limit dispersion relations on trapped-ion quantum hardware

Lucas Marti Email: lucas.marti@fau.de Affiliation: Department of Physics, Friedrich-Alexander Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU), Staudtstraße 7, 91058 Erlangen    Sumeet Email: sumeet.sumeet@fau.de Affiliation: Department of Physics, Friedrich-Alexander Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU), Staudtstraße 7, 91058 Erlangen    Stefan Wolf Affiliation: Department of Physics, Friedrich-Alexander Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU), Staudtstraße 7, 91058 Erlangen    K. P. Schmidt Affiliation: Department of Physics, Friedrich-Alexander Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU), Staudtstraße 7, 91058 Erlangen    Michael J. Hartmann Affiliation: Department of Physics, Friedrich-Alexander Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU), Staudtstraße 7, 91058 Erlangen Affiliation: Quint Computing GmbH, 91058 Erlangen, Germany
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We run a numerical linked-cluster expansion with a quantum algorithm (NLCE+QA), computing ground-state energies and one quasi-particle dispersions in the thermodynamic limit using a 20-qubit trapped-ion quantum processing unit (QPU). The NLCE+QA framework extracts thermodynamic-limit properties from small-cluster calculations, making it naturally suited for near-term quantum devices. Projector-based block-diagonalization schemes such as projective cluster-additive transformation (PCAT) are essential to NLCE+QA, and they involve matrix inversion and square root operations that amplify measurement noise. A central question is therefore whether current hardware can provide expectation values that are accurate enough to withstand non-linear classical post-processing. We explore this challenge for the transverse-field Ising model (TFIM) in one dimension, on a ladder geometry, as well as in a longitudinal field in one dimension. For the quantum algorithm, we consider adiabatic state preparation (ASP), as well as a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) trained on a classical device. The final expectation values are obtained from the QPU, using a novel alternative to the Hadamard test that we name the CX-test. We explore the regimes currently attainable on quantum devices and comment on the improvements needed for quantum computers to achieve results beyond classical reach.

I Introduction

Computing properties of quantum many-body systems in the thermodynamic limit is of central interest in condensed matter physics, yet classical methods face fundamental limitations for strongly correlated systems. Quantum computers offer a promising way forward, but current devices remain constrained in both qubit number and gate fidelity, restricting direct calculations to small system sizes far from the thermodynamic limit.

Methods like numerical linked-cluster expansions (NLCEs) [31, 38] bridge this gap by providing a systematic route to estimating properties of large systems in the thermodynamic limit from calculations on small clusters alone. The method decomposes extensive quantities into contributions from connected clusters via an inclusion-exclusion principle, and is naturally suited for integration with current quantum hardware, since only small clusters serve as input. While dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) also approximates the thermodynamic limit, single-site DMFT lacks spatial correlations and is best suited to high-dimensional lattices [23, 43]; cluster extensions partially restore short-range correlations but remain limited in scope. Tensor network methods such as infinite projected entangled pair states (iPEPS) [17] provide an alternative route to thermodynamic-limit properties that naturally incorporate spatial correlations.

Our approach combines NLCEs with quantum algorithms, where either ASP [1] or a VQE [28] can be used as the quantum algorithm, in the second case resulting in a hybrid quantum-classical framework. Ref. [35] introduced the NLCE+VQE method, in which a classical simulation of this method was applied to calculate the ground-state energy of the TFIM in the thermodynamic limit. In a subsequent work [36], this approach was extended to compute quasi-particle excitation energies. Unlike ground-state energies, excitation energies are encoded in a matrix rather than a single scalar quantity. This introduces additional hurdles. In particular, ensuring cluster additivity becomes a central challenge, which we ensure by the projective cluster-additive transformation (PCAT) [14].

In this work, we present the first hardware implementation of the NLCE+VQE framework proposed in [35, 36], and introduce the NLCE+ASP framework, computing one quasi-particle (1QP) dispersions in the thermodynamic limit on a 20-qubit trapped-ion QPU. A central challenge in bringing this method to real hardware revolves around the capacity of current devices to provide expectation values that are accurate enough for the non-linear classical post-processing inherent in projector-based block-diagonalization schemes such as PCAT, which involves matrix inversion and matrix square root operations. This non-linear structure is not specific to PCAT but is shared by other block-diagonalization approaches such as the Schrieffer-Wolff (SW) transformation; PCAT additionally guarantees cluster additivity, which is required for the NLCE to converge. More broadly, non-linear functions of multiple expectation values pose a generic challenge for noisy quantum devices. On classical computers, operations such as matrix inversions [11] or fractional powers [22] are routine and arise naturally across many areas of physics [19, 32], and thus must be part of any simulation thereof. On noisy quantum hardware, however, the sensitivity of non-linear functions to noise [21] makes their use far less straightforward. Similar questions arise in classical computations that have a stochastic component, for instance variational Monte Carlo [6, 13].

Non-linear processing of quantum data has already been explored in other contexts. In a recent work by Schiffer et al. [33], a Hadamard test is performed iteratively, and the final value is obtained by classically computing a product of fractions g=gngn−1⋯g1g0g=\frac{g_{n}}{g_{n-1}}\cdots\frac{g_{1}}{g_{0}}, where all gjg_{j}, j∈1,…,nj\in 1,\ldots,n, are expectation values obtained from the quantum computer. In such a non-linear combination, the propagation of uncertainty must be carefully controlled, especially when the gjg_{j} are small. Nonetheless, this example finely illustrates that combining expectation values non-linearly can bring out novel algorithmic strategies. It is then natural to ask whether current QPUs have low enough error rates to be integrated into algorithms that make systematic use of non-linear post-processing, while also being able to sample enough to collect sufficient statistics.

We study the challenges that arise when computing the 1QP dispersion in the thermodynamic limit on a QPU, using the NLCE+QA procedure, and mitigate them by introducing a novel alternative to the Hadamard test. Our results, obtained for the polarized phase of the TFIM in one dimension, in a longitudinal field, and on the ladder geometry, indicate that, in limited regimes, the non-linear post-processing pipeline is viable on current hardware, producing recognizable dispersion relations that approach the expected behavior.

Our work opens the door to thermodynamic-limit computation with spatial correlations performed on a QPU, and it addresses a relevant problem in condensed matter physics, for which quantum devices could yield advantages over classical methods. It also indicates that quantum hardware precisions have reached a stage where it becomes meaningful to seek new algorithms that involve non-linear classical post-processing of quantum data.

We note that there is an important distinction between non-linear classical post-processing of sets of expectations, and non-linear functions of quantum states. The former is a hybrid quantum-classical scheme, suited for noisy devices, while the latter directly reflects a physical quantity. The simplest example of these is von Neumann entropy, which can be computed, for example, with block-encodings [41], or classical shadows [15].

As hardware rapidly improves and the transition between NISQ and fault-tolerance [9] broadens the scope of possible algorithms, hybrid approaches pairing quantum measurements with non-linear classical post-processing offer a promising path forward.

The remainder of this work is organized as follows. In Sec. II, we describe the theoretical framework for computing the 1QP dispersion on quantum hardware, including the block-diagonalization strategies (Sec. II.1), the PCAT construction and non-linear post-processing (Sec. II.2), the measurement schemes for matrix elements (Sec. II.3), and the NLCE embedding (Sec. II.5). In Sec. III, we discuss the effect of shot and hardware noise on the results. In Sec. IV, we present the hardware results for the different TFIM models that we picked. We finally discuss future work in Sec. V.

II Approach

Our goal is to compute the 1QP dispersion ω⁡(k→)\omega(\vec{k}) of a quantum spin Hamiltonian of the form H=H0+x​VH=H_{0}+xV, in the thermodynamic limit on quantum hardware using a numerical linked-cluster expansion. Here, k→\vec{k} is the momentum of the quasi-particle and the H0H_{0} term is exactly solvable with a non-degenerate ground state. It can thus be written in a block-diagonal form with respect to QP sectors. To find ω⁡(k→)\omega(\vec{k}), we implement a unitary UU that block-diagonalizes HH for x>0x>0, decoupling the 1QP sector from all other quasi-particle sectors. When doing so, we assume that the dressed QP at finite xx is adiabatically connected to the undressed limit x→0x\rightarrow 0, i.e., there is no quantum phase transition along the way and no quasi-particle decay occurs at any momentum.

The NLCE framework allows for the determination of physical quantities in the thermodynamic limit by performing calculations on finite connected clusters which are appropriately embedded in the infinite system. In the following we first present all relevant information for the treatment of clusters using quantum algorithms and then turn to explain the NLCE scheme.

II.1 Decoupling 1QP using quantum algorithms on clusters

In this subsection, we discuss how to implement quantum algorithms as cluster solvers within the NLCE framework on quantum hardware, including the block-diagonalization strategies, the non-linear post-processing required by the PCAT, and the measurement schemes needed to obtain the necessary matrix elements from the quantum device.

In what follows, all quantities are therefore defined on a single finite cluster CC with NN spins. The extension to the thermodynamic limit via the NLCE is described in Sec. II.5.

We consider the Hamiltonian of the form H=H0+x​VH=H_{0}+xV. Let us stress again that the perturbation x​VxV is assumed to be small enough so that no phase transition and no quasi-particle decay has occurred for smaller values of the perturbation in the thermodynamic limit, i.e. the 1QP excitations always correspond to dressed spin-flip excitations above the paramagnetic ground state. On a finite cluster CC, we exclude the situation of level crossings of the 0QP and 1QP states with states having a larger QP number.

A block-diagonalizing transformation UU satisfies

Heff=U†​H​U=⨁nHeff[n​n],H_{\text{eff}}=U^{\dagger}HU=\bigoplus_{n}H_{\text{eff}}^{[nn]}, (1)

where each block Heff[n​n]H_{\text{eff}}^{[nn]} acts within the nnQP sector. The effective 1QP Hamiltonian is then

Heff[1]=Heff[11]−E[0],H_{\text{eff}}^{[1]}=H_{\text{eff}}^{[11]}-E^{[0]}, (2)

where E[0]E^{[0]} is the ground-state energy. Subtracting E[0]E^{[0]} removes the extensive ground-state contribution: for disconnected clusters A∪BA\cup B, a 1QP excitation on BB carries total energy EA[0]+EB[1]E^{[0]}_{A}+E^{[1]}_{B} and subtracting E[0]=EA[0]+EB[0]E^{[0]}=E_{A}^{[0]}+E_{B}^{[0]} yields the excitation energy on B alone. This makes Heff[1]H^{[1]}_{\text{eff}} an intensive quantity, encoding the one quasi-particle excitation energy which does not scale with system size. Without this subtraction, the reduced contribution of a disconnected cluster A∪BA\cup B would not vanish, and the NLCE would diverge when taking increasingly larger clusters into account.

II.1.1 Quantum algorithms

One way to realize such a block-diagonalizing unitary is via a (quasi) adiabatic transform that mixes states within the same quasi-particle sector but not across different sectors. For an undressed Hamiltonian H0=∑jZjH_{0}=\sum_{j}Z_{j}, the 1QP sector corresponds to spin-flip excitations, i.e. computational basis states having Hamming weight one, and is therefore trivially block-diagonal. In the full Hamiltonian HH, the 1QP sector no longer consists of simple computational basis states with Hamming weight one. Instead, each dressed 1QP state is a superposition that includes contributions from states with higher Hamming weights, reflecting the quantum fluctuations introduced by the perturbation x​VxV. However, under our assumptions, it can be identified entirely through the adiabatic connection and we can define the dressed 1QP sector to be the set of states that are adiabatically connected to the 1QP states of the undressed Hamiltonian H0H_{0}, which we already know.

As we have just described, the block-diagonalization can be most directly implemented on a quantum computer via ASP. Given two adiabatically-connected eigenstates, |Φi[1]⟩|\Phi_{i}^{[1]}\rangle of H0H_{0} and |Ψi[1]⟩|\Psi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle of HH, ASP performs a unitary transform between the two,

|Ψi[1]⟩=limT→∞UASP​(T)​|Φi[1]⟩.\displaystyle|\Psi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle=\lim_{T\rightarrow\infty}U_{\rm ASP}(T)|\Phi_{i}^{[1]}\rangle. (3)

Its accuracy depends on the runtime TT of the overall algorithm, which in turn is governed by the minimum energy gap to the nearest non-degenerate eigenstate along the path [1]. If the time lower bound is not respected, the sweep will leak into nearby states. In our case, the PCAT does not require the final state to be a perfect eigenstate, but a combination of the eigenstates of the correct sector, so that we may rather use

|χi⟩=UASP​(T~)​|Φi[1]⟩=∑i​ℓαi​ℓ​|Ψℓ[1]⟩,|\chi_{i}\rangle=U_{\rm ASP}(\tilde{T})|\Phi_{i}^{[1]}\rangle=\sum_{i\ell}\alpha_{i\ell}|\Psi^{[1]}_{\ell}\rangle, (4)

where T~\tilde{T} is a shorter time that allows mixing 1QP states but not sectors; this somewhat relaxes the runtime constraint.

On a digital device, the sweep unitary UASPU_{\rm ASP} is discretized in time steps, where each time step is typically decomposed in Trotter steps [37], and the Trotter step unitaries can be implemented via a standard Pauli exponential decomposition [26].

Current quantum computers do not have error rates that are low enough to sustain algorithms as deep as ASP whose runtime respects the inverse gap condition [1]. QPU results of the sweep, shown in Fig. 6, hint that the NLCE+ASP pipeline is not yet attainable, and we must find shallower circuits. We describe the case of ASP in detail in App. B, and furthermore estimate the noise regime in which ASP becomes viable.

An alternative approach to NLCE+ASP is NLCE+VQE [35, 36]. In this approach, we want to find a variational circuit UVQE​(θ)U_{\text{VQE}}(\theta) that approximately block-diagonalizes HH by decoupling the ground-state and 1QP sector from higher excitations.

The variational circuit we use is based on the Hamiltonian variational ansatz (HVA) [42], which incorporates the structure of the problem Hamiltonian. For a Hamiltonian decomposed as H=∑jαj​PjH=\sum_{j}\alpha_{j}P_{j}, where PjP_{j} are Pauli strings and αj\alpha_{j} the corresponding coefficients, the HVA applies each term as a parametrized rotation, leading to the unitary,

UHVA​(θ)=∏l=1L∏jexp⁡(i​θj,l​Pj).U_{\mathrm{HVA}}(\theta)=\prod_{l=1}^{L}\prod_{j}\exp\left({\rm i}\,\theta_{j,l}\,P_{j}\right). (5)

A single layer consists of a sequential application of the exponentials exp⁡(i​θj,l​Pj)\exp({\rm i}\,\theta_{j,l}\,P_{j}) for each term PjP_{j} in the Hamiltonian (see for instance Fig. 1) and the full ansatz is obtained by repeating LL layers with independent parameters. This construction is motivated by the Trotter decomposition of an adiabatic sweep: each layer resembles a discrete time step of the sweep, with the variational parameters replacing the fixed schedule. Unless otherwise noted, all the VQEs in this work make use of the HVA ansatz with ⌈N/2⌉\lceil N/2\rceil layers, which was found to be the optimal number for the TFIM on one-dimensional chain and square lattice [35]. The unitary UVQEU_{\rm VQE} is then given by UHVAU_{\mathrm{HVA}} with the optimized parameters, UVQE=UHVA​(θopt)U_{\rm VQE}=U_{\mathrm{HVA}}(\theta_{\rm opt}).

The NLCE+VQE implementation for 1QP requires a cost function that drives UHVAU_{\mathrm{HVA}} towards block-diagonalization. We use the energy variance over the 1QP sector. The key property is that for any quantum state |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle, the energy variance ⟨H2⟩−⟨H⟩2\langle H^{2}\rangle-\langle H\rangle^{2} vanishes if and only if |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle is an eigenstate of HH, or more generally, lies within a degenerate eigenspace [36]. For our purpose, we do not need UHVAU_{\rm HVA} to fully diagonalize HH within the 1QP sector, but only to decouple the 1QP sector from the rest of the spectrum. To this end, we minimize the total variance summed over all transformed 1QP basis states through a cost function defined as,

Cvar1​Q​P​(θ)\displaystyle C_{\mathrm{var}}^{1\mathrm{QP}}(\theta) =∑i=1N⟨Φi[1]|UHVA†​(θ)​H2​UHVA​(θ)|Φi[1]⟩\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\langle\Phi^{[1]}_{i}|\,U_{\rm HVA}^{\dagger}(\theta)\,H^{2}\,U_{\rm HVA}(\theta)|\Phi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle (6)
−∑i,j=1N|⟨Φi[1]|UHVA†(θ)HUHVA(θ)|Φj[1]⟩|2,\displaystyle-\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}\bigl|\langle\Phi^{[1]}_{i}|\,U_{\rm HVA}^{\dagger}(\theta)\,H\,U_{\rm HVA}(\theta)|\Phi^{[1]}_{j}\rangle\bigr|^{2}\,,

where the |Φi[1]⟩|\Phi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle denote the undressed 1QP basis states and NN is the number of sites in the cluster. To see why this cost function achieves block-diagonalization, let us, by analogy to Eq. (4), also denote the prepared 1QP states by |χi⟩=UHVA​|Φi[1]⟩|\chi_{i}\rangle=U_{\rm HVA}|\Phi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle; they are also superpositions of |Ψi[1]⟩|\Psi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle. Since UHVAU_{\rm HVA} is unitary, we can extend {|χi⟩}i=1N\{|\chi_{i}\rangle\}_{i=1}^{N} to a complete orthonormal basis {|χα⟩}\{|\chi_{\alpha}\rangle\} of the full Hilbert space. Inserting the resolution of identity 𝟙=∑α|χα⟩​⟨χα|\mathds{1}=\sum_{\alpha}|\chi_{\alpha}\rangle\langle\chi_{\alpha}| into the first term of Eq. (6),

∑i=1N⟨χi|H2|χi⟩\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{N}\langle\chi_{i}|H^{2}|\chi_{i}\rangle =∑i=1N⟨χi|H⁡(∑α|χα⟩​⟨χα|)​H|χi⟩\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\langle\chi_{i}|H\left(\sum_{\alpha}|\chi_{\alpha}\rangle\langle\chi_{\alpha}|\right)H|\chi_{i}\rangle
=∑i=1N∑α|⟨χα|H|χi⟩|2\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{\alpha}\bigl|\langle\chi_{\alpha}|H|\chi_{i}\rangle\bigr|^{2}
=∑i=1N∑α∈1​Q​P|⟨χα|H|χi⟩|2\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{\alpha\in\mathrm{1QP}}\bigl|\langle\chi_{\alpha}|H|\chi_{i}\rangle\bigr|^{2}
+∑i=1N∑α∉1​Q​P|⟨χα|H|χi⟩|2.\displaystyle\quad\quad\quad+\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{\alpha\notin\mathrm{1QP}}\bigl|\langle\chi_{\alpha}|H|\chi_{i}\rangle\bigr|^{2}. (7)

The first sum on the right-hand side is exactly the second term in Eq. (6), since α∈1​Q​P\alpha\in\mathrm{1QP} runs over j=1,…,Nj=1,\ldots,N. Substituting back, the two terms cancel and the cost function reduces to

Cvar1​Q​P​(𝜽)=∑i=1N∑α∉1​Q​P|⟨χα|H|χi⟩|2.C_{\mathrm{var}}^{\mathrm{1QP}}(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{\alpha\notin\mathrm{1QP}}\bigl|\langle\chi_{\alpha}|H|\chi_{i}\rangle\bigr|^{2}. (8)

This sum vanishes if and only if every matrix element of HH connecting the transformed 1QP sector to the rest of the Hilbert space is zero, i.e., the transformed 1QP sector is an invariant subspace of HH, meaning that HH maps this subspace onto itself. Since both terms in Eq. (6) depend only on the subspace spanned by {|χi⟩}\{|\chi_{i}\rangle\} and not on the choice of basis within it, Cvar1​Q​PC_{\mathrm{var}}^{\mathrm{1QP}} is invariant under rotations within the 1QP block [36].

Furthermore, the ground-state energy E[0]E^{[0]}, as shown in Eq. (2), must also be measured. Either the same adiabatic sweep as mentioned before can be used for this purpose, or another VQE trained using a standard energy-minimizing cost function [29] given as,

CE​(θ)=⟨Φ[0]|UHVA†​(θ)​H​UHVA​(θ)|Φ[0]⟩,\displaystyle C_{E}(\theta)=\langle\Phi^{[0]}|U_{\rm HVA}^{\dagger}(\theta)HU_{\rm HVA}(\theta)|\Phi^{[0]}\rangle, (9)

can be used to obtain the ground-state energy. In this work, we compute the ground-state energy using sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), as explained in Sec. II.3.1.

II.2 Non-linear processing on clusters

An exact block-diagonalizing unitary is not unique: for degenerate subspaces, infinitely many unitaries achieve the same decoupling. In practice, the unitary UQAU_{\mathrm{QA}} block-diagonalizes HH only approximately but the resulting effective Hamiltonian is not guaranteed to be cluster-additive, a property required for the NLCE to converge. In this section, we describe the PCAT [14] that enforces cluster additivity, and detail how its required matrix elements are obtained from the quantum device.

II.2.1 Projective cluster-additive transformation

In an NLCE, thermodynamic-limit quantities are reconstructed from calculations on small connected clusters via a procedure that converges only if the effective Hamiltonian HeffH_{\mathrm{eff}} on two disconnected clusters AA and BB decomposes as

Heff​(A∪B)=Heff​(A)⊗𝟙B+𝟙A⊗Heff​(B).H_{\mathrm{eff}}(A\cup B)=H_{\mathrm{eff}}(A)\otimes\mathds{1}_{B}+\mathds{1}_{A}\otimes H_{\mathrm{eff}}(B). (10)

Without such cluster additivity, the effective Hamiltonian can contain spurious terms that allow dressed quasi-particles to hop between disconnected clusters, causing the NLCE to diverge with increasing cluster size. Standard block-diagonalization transformations like Schrieffer-Wolff [4] can violate this property, which motivates the process described below.

The PCAT [14] resolves this by constructing a modified unitary UPCATU_{\text{PCAT}} from the QA solution, which preserves Eq. (10) by construction. The key insight is that eigenstates on disconnected clusters A∪BA\cup B have product structure,

|ΨA∪B[n+m]⟩=|ΨA[n]⟩⊗|ΨB[m]⟩.|\Psi_{A\cup B}^{[n+m]}\rangle=|\Psi_{A}^{[n]}\rangle\otimes|\Psi_{B}^{[m]}\rangle. (11)

For ground states on disjoint clusters, this product structure is automatically preserved by any block-diagonalizing transformation, since ground-state additivity,

EA∪B[0]=EA[0]+EB[0],E_{A\cup B}^{[0]}=E_{A}^{[0]}+E_{B}^{[0]}, (12)

always holds for disconnected clusters, which follows from the factorization of the Hamiltonian in Eq. (10). For excited states, however, general unitary transformations UQAU_{\rm QA} mix in ground-state components that break the product structure in Eq. (11). PCAT eliminates this mixing by constructing modified states |Ψ~i[1]⟩|\tilde{\Psi}_{i}^{[1]}\rangle by eliminating projections onto the 0QP sector of H0H_{0},

|Ψ~i[1]⟩=|Ψi[1]⟩−⟨Φ[0]|Ψi[1]⟩⟨Φ[0]|Ψ[0]⟩​|Ψ[0]⟩|\tilde{\Psi}_{i}^{[1]}\rangle=|\Psi_{i}^{[1]}\rangle-\frac{\langle\Phi^{[0]}|\Psi_{i}^{[1]}\rangle}{\langle\Phi^{[0]}|\Psi^{[0]}\rangle}|\Psi^{[0]}\rangle (13)

where |Ψ[0]⟩|\Psi^{[0]}\rangle and |Ψi[1]⟩|\Psi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle are the exact ground-state and 1QP eigenstates of HH, and |Φ[0]⟩|\Phi^{[0]}\rangle is the undressed ground state. Note that Eq. (13) implicitly assumes ⟨Φ[0]|Ψ[0]⟩≠0\langle\Phi^{[0]}|\Psi^{[0]}\rangle\neq 0, which is guaranteed by the adiabatic connection between the dressed and undressed ground states.

As the states |Ψ~i[1]⟩|\tilde{\Psi}^{[1]}_{i}\rangle have zero projection onto the ground-state sector of H0H_{0}, i.e., P0​|Ψ~i[1]⟩=0P_{0}|\tilde{\Psi}^{[1]}_{i}\rangle=0, the product structure on disconnected clusters is restored, |Ψ~A∪Bn+m⟩=|Ψ~An⟩⊗|Ψ~Bm⟩|\tilde{\Psi}^{n+m}_{A\cup B}\rangle=|\tilde{\Psi}^{n}_{A}\rangle\otimes|\tilde{\Psi}^{m}_{B}\rangle, and the overlap matrix between undressed and modified states becomes block-diagonal in the cluster indices. We note that, among the models studied in this work, the modification in Eq. (13) is only needed for the TFIM with a longitudinal field (TFIM+LF). For the remaining models, the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetry enforces ⟨Φ[0]|Ψi[1]⟩=0\langle\Phi^{[0]}|\Psi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle=0, so that |Ψ~i[1]⟩=|Ψi[1]⟩|\tilde{\Psi}^{[1]}_{i}\rangle=|\Psi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle.

The states |Ψ[0]⟩|\Psi^{[0]}\rangle and |Ψi[1]⟩|\Psi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle do not need to be measured directly on the quantum device, but only in expectation values and overlap matrices as we describe in Sec. II.3. Thus, from the modified states |Ψ~i[1]⟩|\tilde{\Psi}^{[1]}_{i}\rangle, we construct the modified overlap matrix [14]

O~i​j[1]=⟨Φi[1]|Ψ~j[1]⟩,\tilde{O}_{ij}^{[1]}=\langle\Phi_{i}^{[1]}|\tilde{\Psi}_{j}^{[1]}\rangle, (14)

and the PCAT correction within the 1QP sector,

V[1]=O~[1]†(O~[1]O~[1]†)−1/2.V^{[1]}=\tilde{O}^{[1]\dagger}\left(\tilde{O}^{[1]}\tilde{O}^{[1]\dagger}\right)^{-1/2}. (15)

Eq. (15) is the symmetric Löwdin orthonormalization of O~[1]†\tilde{O}^{[1]\dagger}, the partial isometry closest to the identity that orthonormalizes the modified states [14]. The effective 1QP Hamiltonian is then

Heff[1]=V[1]†H[1]V[1]−E[0],H_{\text{eff}}^{[1]}=V^{[1]\dagger}H^{[1]}V^{[1]}-E^{[0]}, (16)

where Hi​j[1]=⟨Ψi[1]|H|Ψj[1]⟩H^{[1]}_{ij}=\langle\Psi^{[1]}_{i}|H|\Psi^{[1]}_{j}\rangle. By construction, V[1]V^{[1]} inherits the block-diagonal structure of O~[1]\tilde{O}^{[1]} on disconnected clusters, guaranteeing that the resulting Heff[1]H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff}} satisfies Eq. (10). We note that the matrix inversion and square root in Eq. (15) are the non-linear operations that we mentioned earlier.

II.2.2 Computing PCAT on quantum hardware

The final result V[1]†H[1]V[1]V^{[1]\dagger}H^{[1]}V^{[1]} in Eq. (16) depends on O~[1]\tilde{O}^{[1]} only through the combinations O~[1]O~[1]†\tilde{O}^{[1]}\tilde{O}^{[1]\dagger} and O~[1]H~[1]O~[1]†\tilde{O}^{[1]}\tilde{H}^{[1]}\tilde{O}^{[1]\dagger}, which are unchanged if one rotates the basis within the 1QP sector [14]. In practice, this means that the states prepared by the QA do not need to be eigenstates of HH; it is sufficient that they span the correct subspace. We can therefore use the QA-prepared states |χi⟩|\chi_{i}\rangle directly in Eqs. (13)-(16) without requiring any additional orthonormalization step.

The corresponding implementation of Eq. (13) reads

|χ~i[1]⟩=|χi[1]⟩−⟨Φ[0]|χi[1]⟩⟨Φ[0]|χ[0]⟩​|χ[0]⟩,|\tilde{\chi}^{[1]}_{i}\rangle=|\chi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle-\frac{\langle\Phi^{[0]}|\chi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle}{\langle\Phi^{[0]}|\chi^{[0]}\rangle}|\chi^{[0]}\rangle, (17)

where |χ[0]⟩|\chi^{[0]}\rangle and |χi[1]⟩|\chi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle are the ground-state and 1QP states prepared by the quantum algorithm. This substitution is justified by the subspace invariance: the PCAT result depends only on the subspace spanned by the prepared states, not on whether they are exact eigenstates.

The PCAT construction in Eq. (16) requires two sets of measurements from the quantum device, each forming an (N+1)×(N+1)(N+1)\times(N+1) matrix for a cluster of NN sites.

The ground-state energy is computed independently (see Sec. II.3.1). Therefore, in order to build the PCAT construction in Eq. (16), we only need to measure the ground-state energy and two N×NN\times N matrices corresponding to the 1QP sector. These two matrices are as follows.

  1. 1.

    Hamiltonian matrix HH: Here, the elements Hi​j=⟨Φi[1]|UQA†​H​UQA|Φj[1]⟩H_{ij}=\langle\Phi_{i}^{[1]}|U^{\dagger}_{\rm QA}HU_{\rm QA}|\Phi_{j}^{[1]}\rangle =⟨χi[1]|H|χj[1]⟩=\langle\chi_{i}^{[1]}|H|\chi_{j}^{[1]}\rangle are in the QA-prepared state basis. The diagonal elements are standard expectation values, whereas off-diagonal elements require measurements on pairwise superpositions of computational basis states, as we explain in the next section.

  2. 2.

    Overlap matrix O~\tilde{O}: Elements O~i​j=⟨Φi[1]|χ~j[1]⟩\tilde{O}_{ij}=\langle\Phi^{[1]}_{i}|\tilde{\chi}_{j}^{[1]}\rangle quantify the overlap between undressed eigenstates |Φi[1]⟩|\Phi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle and modified QA-prepared states |χ~i[1]⟩|\tilde{\chi}^{[1]}_{i}\rangle. These are constructed by preparing the QA-prepared states |χi[1]⟩|\chi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle, and applying the correction in Eq. (17) if it is needed. The correction is computed separately as described in Sec. II.4. Both can be measured using the Hadamard or the CX-test described in Sec. II.3.3.

The total measurement cost scales as 𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}), which is the number of matrix elements per cluster. In the case of VQE, these measurements are performed only after optimization is complete, and the subsequent PCAT construction and NLCE embedding proceed entirely classically, since all matrices are of quadratic size with respect to the number of spins NN in the Hamiltonian.

II.3 Measuring matrix elements on a quantum device

We have described three sorts of measurements that we require from the quantum device; each needs its own treatment.

II.3.1 Ground-state energy

For the calculation of the ground-state energy, we train the VQE on a classical computer, with an energy minimization cost function, as in Eq. (9). For ASP, which we use as well, no training is required. On the quantum device, we then sample the state obtained with the quantum circuit in the ZZ-basis, and perform sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) [18, 34], which consists of building the sub-matrix of the Hamiltonian in the subspace formed by the sampled computational basis states, and classically diagonalizing that matrix. This works particularly well when the ground state consists of a superposition of a polynomial number of computational basis states. Hence, assuming that the ground state |E0⟩|E_{0}\rangle of some NN-qubit Hamiltonian H^\hat{H} can be well approximated by a linear combination of MM computational basis states, and that all these have been sampled in the data acquisition phase, we need to diagonalize an M×MM\times M matrix.

By the variational principle, its lowest eigenvalue upper bounds the ground-state energy of H^\hat{H}, and the bound tightens as the support of the ground state on the sampled bitstrings increases.

II.3.2 Hamiltonian matrix

Beyond the ground-state energy, we must measure off-diagonal Hamiltonian elements Hi​j=⟨Φi[1]|U†​H​U|Φj[1]⟩H_{ij}=\langle\Phi_{i}^{[1]}|U^{\dagger}HU|\Phi_{j}^{[1]}\rangle for i,j=1,…,Ni,j=1,...,N. Here UU denotes any unitary acting on the full 2N2^{N} Hilbert space, either VQE or ASP. Recall that |Φj[1]⟩|\Phi_{j}^{[1]}\rangle are Hamming weight one computational basis states, |Φj[1]⟩=Xj​|0⟩⊗N|\Phi_{j}^{[1]}\rangle=X_{j}|0\rangle^{\otimes N}, where XjX_{j} is the Pauli XX matrix acting on the jjth qubit. In the general case of any Hamiltonian and any pair of states whose superposition we can prepare, it is possible to extract two off-diagonal elements from four expectation values. Consider the expectation values

γ1\displaystyle\gamma_{1} =12​(⟨Φi[1]|+⟨Φj[1]|)​U†​H​U​(|Φi[1]⟩+|Φj[1]⟩)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}(\langle\Phi^{[1]}_{i}|+\langle\Phi^{[1]}_{j}|)U^{\dagger}HU(|\Phi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle+|\Phi^{[1]}_{j}\rangle)
γ2\displaystyle\gamma_{2} =12​(⟨Φi[1]|−⟨Φj[1]|)​U†​H​U​(|Φi[1]⟩−|Φj[1]⟩)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}(\langle\Phi^{[1]}_{i}|-\langle\Phi^{[1]}_{j}|)U^{\dagger}HU(|\Phi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle-|\Phi^{[1]}_{j}\rangle)
γ3\displaystyle\gamma_{3} =12​(⟨Φi[1]|−i⁡⟨Φj[1]|)​U†​H​U​(|Φi[1]⟩+i⁡|Φj[1]⟩)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}(\langle\Phi^{[1]}_{i}|-{\rm i}\langle\Phi^{[1]}_{j}|)U^{\dagger}HU(|\Phi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle+{\rm i}|\Phi^{[1]}_{j}\rangle)
γ4\displaystyle\gamma_{4} =12​(⟨Φi[1]|+i⁡⟨Φj[1]|)​U†​H​U​(|Φi[1]⟩−i⁡|Φj[1]⟩)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}(\langle\Phi^{[1]}_{i}|+{\rm i}\langle\Phi^{[1]}_{j}|)U^{\dagger}HU(|\Phi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle-{\rm i}|\Phi^{[1]}_{j}\rangle)

where we recall that (|Φi[1]⟩−i⁡|Φj[1]⟩)†=⟨Φi[1]|+i⁡⟨Φj[1]|(|\Phi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle-{\rm i}|\Phi^{[1]}_{j}\rangle)^{\dagger}=\langle\Phi^{[1]}_{i}|+{\rm i}\langle\Phi^{[1]}_{j}|. Then

γ1−γ2\displaystyle\gamma_{1}-\gamma_{2} =2​R​e​⟨Φi[1]|U†​H​U|Φj[1]⟩\displaystyle=2\mathrm{Re}\langle\Phi^{[1]}_{i}|U^{\dagger}HU|\Phi^{[1]}_{j}\rangle
−i⁡(γ3−γ4)\displaystyle-{\rm i}(\gamma_{3}-\gamma_{4}) =2​I​m​⟨Φi[1]|U†​H​U|Φj[1]⟩,\displaystyle=2\mathrm{Im}\langle\Phi^{[1]}_{i}|U^{\dagger}HU|\Phi^{[1]}_{j}\rangle,

Due to the Hermiticity of the matrix, only half of the off-diagonal elements need to be computed.

The superposition (|Φi[1]⟩+|Φj[1]⟩)/2(|\Phi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle+|\Phi^{[1]}_{j}\rangle)/\sqrt{2} can be built with Xi​CNOTi​j​Hi​|0⟩⊗NX_{i}\,{\mathrm{CNOT}}_{ij}\,H_{i}|0\rangle^{\otimes N}, and likewise for the three other superpositions.

II.3.3 Overlap matrix

Finally, we must compute overlaps between states, or, in other words, off-diagonal elements of a unitary, in order to build the overlap matrix O~i​j=⟨Φi[1]|χ~j[1]⟩\tilde{O}_{ij}=\langle\Phi^{[1]}_{i}|\tilde{\chi}^{[1]}_{j}\rangle, where |χ~j[1]⟩|\tilde{\chi}^{[1]}_{j}\rangle is the QA-prepared superposition as defined in Eq. (17) with the PCAT correction applied. When ⟨Φ[0]|χi[1]⟩=0\langle\Phi^{[0]}|\chi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle=0, the elements we compute reduce to ⟨Φi[1]|χj[1]⟩=⟨Φi[1]|UQA|Φj[1]⟩\langle\Phi^{[1]}_{i}|\chi^{[1]}_{j}\rangle=\langle\Phi^{[1]}_{i}|U_{\rm QA}|\Phi^{[1]}_{j}\rangle.

For any unitary UU, this can usually be done with the well-known Hadamard test, which we summarize for completeness in App. D. The main disadvantage of this test is that it requires us to implement a controlled version of UU, and this might make the circuit very deep. For PCAT, however, the controlled unitary can be avoided entirely, reducing the cost of controlled unitaries to two CX gates per matrix element. Consider the circuit in Fig. 2.

In that circuit, we select for the all-zeros state in the system register, and measure the ancilla as in the Hadamard test. In what follows, |0⟩⊗N≡|0⟩|0\rangle^{\otimes N}\equiv|0\rangle for clarity. The expectation of the composite state of the ancilla and system is

⟨μ′|(X⊗|0⟩​⟨0|)|μ′⟩\displaystyle\langle\mu^{\prime}|(X\otimes|0\rangle\langle 0|)|\mu^{\prime}\rangle =12[⟨0|U†|0⟩⟨0|XiUXj|0⟩+h.c.]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left[\langle 0|U^{\dagger}|0\rangle\langle 0|X_{i}UX_{j}|0\rangle+h.c.\right]
=Re⁡(⟨0|U†|0⟩​⟨Φi[1]|U|Φj[1]⟩),\displaystyle=\mathrm{Re}\left(\langle 0|U^{\dagger}|0\rangle\langle\Phi^{[1]}_{i}|U|\Phi^{[1]}_{j}\rangle\right),

where we defined

|μ′⟩\displaystyle|\mu^{\prime}\rangle =12​[|0A⟩​U​|0⟩+|1A⟩​Xi​U​Xj​|0⟩],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left[|0_{A}\rangle U|0\rangle+|1_{A}\rangle X_{i}UX_{j}|0\rangle\right],

to be the output state of the circuit before the measurement. We immediately notice that this circuit gives us the desired matrix element multiplied by a scalar ⟨0|U†|0⟩\langle 0|U^{\dagger}|0\rangle. This means we only need to measure this scalar once, using the Hadamard test, and the rest of the N2N^{2} values can be computed using the cheaper CX-test described above. This is particularly useful when a polynomial amount of matrix elements need to be computed. It can also be straightforwardly extended to the imaginary part of the matrix element.

As we mentioned above, in the specific case of PCAT, we can also avoid computing ⟨0|U†|0⟩\langle 0|U^{\dagger}|0\rangle entirely, allowing us to avoid any use of the Hadamard test. To see this, consider again the PCAT correction defined in Eq. (15), and the resulting effective Hamiltonian. Assuming we use the resulting matrix directly from the CX-test, i.e. multiplied by ⟨0|U†|0⟩\langle 0|U^{\dagger}|0\rangle, we get

⟨0|U|0⟩⟨0|U†|0⟩​V[1],\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{\langle 0|U|0\rangle}{\langle 0|U^{\dagger}|0\rangle}}V^{[1]}\,, (18)

and the resulting prefactors cancel in Eq. (16). Therefore, we do not need to compute ⟨0|U†|0⟩\langle 0|U^{\dagger}|0\rangle at all. Hence, we can entirely skip the expensive Hadamard tests, and simply perform the CX-tests. Still, we will see that, even with this improvement, ASP on current hardware does not produce results as accurate as those produced by the VQE.

We note the similarity between our CX-test and the iterative Hadamard test and related algorithms independently discovered by Schiffer et al. [33]. While their approach also reduces the number of controlled gates needed for overlap estimation, the CX-test is more efficient in the PCAT setting because the global prefactor ⟨0|U†|0⟩\langle 0|U^{\dagger}|0\rangle cancels in the final product V[1]†H[1]V[1]V^{[1]\dagger}H^{[1]}V^{[1]}, eliminating the need to measure it altogether.

Apart from the above mentioned measurements, we note that VQE training itself requires evaluating the cost function Eq. (6) on hardware, adding to the total measurement budget. In this work, however, all VQE optimizations are performed on a classical computer, therefore we measure only the final matrix elements on the QPU. Our goal is to demonstrate the possibility of performing the NLCE+QA set up on a quantum device which includes the non-linear PCAT. As quantum hardware improves, it will become possible to replace the VQE with ASP, which performs the same block-diagonalizing function while forgoing the training process and sidestepping associated challenges such as barren plateaus [20].

II.4 Treatment of mixing between 0QP and 1QP

When the overlap ⟨Φ[0]|χj[1]⟩\langle\Phi^{[0]}|\chi^{[1]}_{j}\rangle is non-zero, the second term in Eq. (17) does not vanish. Hence, elements of O~i​j\tilde{O}_{ij} cannot be simply computed using ⟨Φi[1]|U|Φj[1]⟩\langle\Phi^{[1]}_{i}|U|\Phi^{[1]}_{j}\rangle, but we must now take the second term of Eq. (17) into account. Substituting |χj[n]⟩=U⁡|Φj[n]⟩,n∈{0,1}|\chi^{[n]}_{j}\rangle=U|\Phi^{[n]}_{j}\rangle,n\in\{0,1\} and multiplying Eq. (17) by ⟨Φi[1]|\langle\Phi^{[1]}_{i}|, each matrix element is then computed as

O~i​j\displaystyle\tilde{O}_{ij} =⟨Φi[1]|U|Φj[1]⟩−⟨Φ[0]|U|Φj[1]⟩⟨Φ[0]|U|Φ[0]⟩​⟨Φi[1]|U|Φ[0]⟩\displaystyle=\langle\Phi^{[1]}_{i}|U|\Phi^{[1]}_{j}\rangle-\frac{\langle\Phi^{[0]}|U|\Phi_{j}^{[1]}\rangle}{\langle\Phi^{[0]}|U|\Phi^{[0]}\rangle}\langle\Phi^{[1]}_{i}|U|\Phi^{[0]}\rangle
=⟨Φi[1]|U|Φj[1]⟩−Δi​j.\displaystyle=\langle\Phi^{[1]}_{i}|U|\Phi^{[1]}_{j}\rangle-\Delta_{ij}.

Beyond the N2N^{2} terms needed to compute ⟨Φi[1]|U|Φj[1]⟩\langle\Phi^{[1]}_{i}|U|\Phi^{[1]}_{j}\rangle, as we described earlier, we also need to compute three overlaps in the correction that is subtracted from the main term. These can be computed on their own, each with a single CX-test. The phase cancellation, described in Sec. II.3.3, is still valid, and the Hadamard test for ⟨0|U|0⟩\langle 0|U|0\rangle can still be avoided, but one must be careful with the unitaries. While the ASP algorithm identically prepares superpositions of 1QP states as it prepares the ground state, the unitaries in the above equation may differ when using VQEs: the circuit preparing the 1QP states may be different from the one preparing the ground state. This can be circumvented by adding a ground state term to the block-diagonalizing cost function in Eq. (8) that also minimizes the ground-state energy, such that the CX-test phases of the denominator and numerator cancel, and the overall phase is the same as the first term [36].

In total, the correction terms Δi​j\Delta_{ij} require 2​(2​N+1)2(2N+1) more circuits, because their product can be computed independently. Regardless, it turns out that it is impossible to detect this correction Δi​j\Delta_{ij} within our current sampling budget MM, i.e. Δi​j≪1/M\Delta_{ij}\ll 1/\sqrt{M}. Indeed, for the studied TFIM+LF case, we found that Δi​j≈4⋅10−4\Delta_{ij}\approx 4\cdot 10^{-4}, thus requiring about M=5⋅106M=5\cdot 10^{6} shots per element.

II.5 Numerical linked-cluster expansions

The preceding subsections described how to obtain the effective 1QP Hamiltonian on a single finite cluster CC. We now focus on how these finite-cluster results are embedded in the thermodynamic limit within numerical linked-cluster expansions (NLCEs), which provide a systematic scheme for obtaining bulk properties from finite-cluster calculations. The core idea behind NLCEs is to decompose an extensive quantity into contributions from connected clusters using the inclusion-exclusion principle. Reduced contributions are computed on topologically distinct clusters and embedded into the infinite lattice, weighted by the number of embeddings per site.

For a property PP, the reduced contribution of a cluster CC is defined recursively as

P¯C=PC−∑C′⊊CwC′/C​P¯C′,\bar{P}_{C}=P_{C}-\sum_{C^{\prime}\subsetneq C}w_{C^{\prime}/C}\,\bar{P}_{C^{\prime}}, (19)

where wC′/Cw_{C^{\prime}/C} counts embeddings of subcluster C′C^{\prime} within CC. The thermodynamic-limit value is then obtained by summing reduced contributions over all topologically distinct clusters,

P=∑CwC​P¯C,P=\sum_{C}w_{C}\,\bar{P}_{C}, (20)

where wCw_{C} is the embedding weight of cluster CC per lattice site.

For computational efficiency, it is optimal to employ a rectangular graph expansion in which only clusters of dimensions Lm×LnL_{m}\times L_{n} with Lm​Ln≤NmaxL_{m}L_{n}\leq N_{\text{max}} are included. Here NmaxN_{\text{max}} is the number of spins in the largest cluster taken in the NLCE calculation. This restricts the number of clusters to polynomial growth in system size, making the approach tractable for hybrid quantum-classical implementation [36]. In particular, for one-dimensional lattices like the chain and the two-leg ladder investigated in this work, the number of clusters reduces to the two: Nmax×1N_{\text{max}}\times 1 and (Nmax−1)×1(N_{\text{max}}-1)\times 1 for the chain and (Nmax/2)×2(N_{\text{max}}/2)\times 2 and (Nmax−2)/2×2(N_{\text{max}}-2)/2\times 2 for the two-leg ladder.

A critical requirement for NLCE convergence is that the quantity PP be cluster-additive: for any two disconnected clusters AA and BB, the reduced contribution of their union must vanish, P¯A∪B=0\bar{P}_{A\cup B}=0. This property ensures that only connected clusters contribute to the expansion which is guaranteed by PCAT, as explained in section II.2.

For each finite cluster CC, the QA and PCAT procedure described above yields an effective 1QP Hamiltonian Heff[1]H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff}} with real-space matrix elements connecting sites within the cluster. Assuming a one-site unit cell, the 1QP dispersion ω⁡(k→)\omega(\vec{k}) in the thermodynamic limit is then obtained from the NLCE embedding through a Fourier transform,

ω⁡(k→)=∑Lm,Ln∑μ→,ν→ei​k→⋅(ν→−μ→)​H¯eff,Lm×Ln,μ→,ν→[1],\omega(\vec{k})=\sum_{L_{m},L_{n}}\sum_{\vec{\mu},\vec{\nu}}e^{i\vec{k}\cdot(\vec{\nu}-\vec{\mu})}\,\bar{H}^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},L_{m}\times L_{n},\vec{\mu},\vec{\nu}}, (21)

where H¯eff[1]\bar{H}^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff}} denotes the reduced contribution of each cluster, obtained according to Eq. (19), and the outer sum runs over all clusters Lm×LnL_{m}\times L_{n} with weight one included in the NLCE. For a larger unit cell with mm sites, one obtains by the same embedding procedure an m×mm\times m matrix for each momentum k→\vec{k} resulting in mm 1QP bands.

III Error and uncertainty

Because the shot noise, the hardware imperfections, and the non-linear character of the post-processing interact in a nuanced way, it is important to carefully build an understanding of how the uncertainty and the error propagate into the final dispersion obtained by NLCE+QA in the thermodynamic limit. We use the word “uncertainty” to denote the lack of knowledge due to the inevitable need to estimate observables with a finite number of measurements, and “error” to refer to the difference between the ideal value and the imperfect estimate.

III.1 Uncertainty propagation

We first discuss how the final uncertainty in the dispersion relations is calculated, or, in other words, how we obtain statistical uncertainty through the non-linear post-processing. The non-linear character of the PCAT construction, particularly the matrix inverse and square root in (O~[1]O~[1]†)−1/2(\tilde{O}^{[1]}\tilde{O}^{[1]\dagger})^{-1/2}, means that errors propagate in a non-trivial manner and can be amplified significantly if the input data is not sufficiently accurate. Computing the propagation of uncertainty from the initial quantum measurements to the final dispersion relation requires the use of a Monte Carlo simulation [45]. From the expectation values measured on the quantum device, we compute the error-on-the-mean (EOTM) [10, 3], which is defined for each Pauli string PP as σ=(1−⟨P⟩2)/M\sigma=\sqrt{(1-\langle P\rangle^{2})/M}, with MM the number of shots. It gives the best estimates for the variance of the mean value, and is also called the experimental standard deviation of the mean [10].

To analyze the error propagation through our post-processing procedure, we generate random data points (overlap and Hamiltonian matrices) that are distributed according to a Gaussian distribution around the found mean value with variance σ2\sigma^{2}. We then propagate these data points through the NLCE procedure to compute dispersion curve values ω⁡(k→)\omega(\vec{k}) for each of them. This allows us to take the standard deviation of the resulting distribution of ω⁡(k→)\omega(\vec{k})-values as uncertainties for our results

We sample Mmc=104M_{\rm mc}=10^{4} dispersions, based on a study of EOTM convergence shown in App. C.

As matrix sizes increase and Monte Carlo sampling becomes too difficult, one could turn to methods such as the Unscented Transform (UT) [40] to compute the uncertainty propagation at a lower cost. In our case, this would decrease the number of samples needed from about 10410^{4} to 𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}), where NN is the number of qubits. However, the UT has stricter assumptions on the form of the distribution, and may diverge if the function is not smooth enough [40].

For the ground-state energy estimation we use a conservative upper bound h/Mh/\sqrt{M}, with hh as defined in Eq. (24), since the uncertainty in SQD is relative to the distribution of the ground state [18], and not straightforwardly computable as it involves diagonalizing a matrix. Yet, simulations indicate that the value is likely lower.

III.2 Error propagation

Having discussed the uncertainty of our results due to shot noise, we now turn to investigate the influence of gate errors on our results. To analyze these effects we do noisy simulations for different noise levels, and explore their influence on the obtained dispersions. This allows us to investigate which noise level leads to comparable results to those that we obtain from our runs on the real QPU, and helps us determine which number of measurements is needed to determine the dispersion values with good enough accuracy.

Our noisy simulations use the assumption that depolarization noise is the main hardware error channel [5, 39]. This is justified when the circuit has many qubits and gates, as the different errors can be amalgamated into depolarization noise [26]. While one may of course build more advanced error models, which, for example, take non-unital noise into account [25], comparisons with real hardware runs indicate that it is sufficiently justified in terms of experimental performance.

Depolarization noise can be expressed as a quantum channel ℰ\mathcal{E} for an NN-qubit state ρ\rho, written as

ℰ⁡(ρ)=(1−p)​ρ+p​tr​(ρ)​𝟙2N,\displaystyle\mathcal{E}(\rho)=(1-p)\,\rho+p\,\,\mathrm{tr}(\rho)\,\frac{\mathds{1}}{2^{N}}, (22)

where pp is the depolarization rate and 𝟙/2N\mathds{1}/2^{N} describes the maximally mixed state. We analyze the effect of depolarization noise by applying the depolarization channel as given in Eq. (22) after each gate. The effect of this gate-based approach will result in an effective depolarization rate for observables that depends on both the circuit and the observable.

As the emulator for AQT devices uses depolarization rates of p=0.003p=0.003 for single-qubit gates, and p=0.01p=0.01 for two-qubit gates, we take these values as reference (though we note that they are not finetuned to exactly match the particular device we use). In our numerical simulations, we can then increase or decrease these depolarization rates to see how they distort the dispersion relation.

In Fig. 3 we investigate the effect of various levels of depolarization noise on the dispersion that we compute via the non-linear post-processing of the noisy measured data. One can see a tendency of the dispersion curve computed from the data to increasingly shift upwards as the level of depolarization noise increases. This trend becomes more pronounced as we increase the number of shots to reduce the uncertainty in the data.

In our case, the upward bias originates from the way we measure the ground energy using SQD, which gives more accurate results than the other measurements. We obtain the dispersion via Eq. (21), with effective Hamiltonians given by Eq. (16). Now, for a depolarizing channel at the gate level as in Eq. (22), one can obtain an effective depolarization channel for each observable OO on an NN-qubit state ρ\rho as

⟨Onoisy⟩ρ\displaystyle\langle O_{\mathrm{noisy}}\rangle_{\rho} =(1−pO)​⟨Oideal⟩ρ+pO​tr​(O2N),\displaystyle=(1-p_{O})\langle O_{\mathrm{ideal}}\rangle_{\rho}+p_{O}\,\,\mathrm{tr}\big(\frac{O}{2^{N}}\big), (23)

where pOp_{O} is the effective depolarization rate of the observable OO for ρ\rho. In our case, we can assume that the matrix elements of Hi​jH_{ij} have a common effective depolarization rate, which we call pHp_{H}, while Eq. (15) tells us that any depolarization noise in the overlap matrix cancels. The SQD technique allows us to get a much more accurate energy estimate than direct estimation. We can thus assume an effective depolarization rate pEp_{E} for the ground state energy that is smaller than pHp_{H}, and write pH=pE+δp_{H}=p_{E}+\delta with δ>0\delta>0.

Hence, the depolarized effective Hamiltonian can be taken to read

Heff,noisy[1]\displaystyle H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff,noisy}} =(1−pH)V[1]†H[1]V[1]−(1−pE)E[0]\displaystyle=(1-p_{H})V^{[1]\dagger}H^{[1]}V^{[1]}-(1-p_{E})E^{[0]}
=(1−pH)​Heff[1]−δ​E[0],\displaystyle=(1-p_{H})H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff}}-\delta E^{[0]},

where we used pE=pH−δp_{E}=p_{H}-\delta. In the resulting dispersion given by Eq. (21), we can take the constant −δ​E[0]-\delta E^{[0]} contribution out of the sum, since it acts on the diagonal. As the ground state energy E[0]E^{[0]} is always negative for the systems we study, the constant −δ​E[0]-\delta E^{[0]} pushes the overall dispersion upwards. In turn, the 1−pH1-p_{H} factor, which contributes with various phase prefactors, compresses the vertical spread dispersion, as we see most illustratively in the bottom left panel of Fig. 3. In fact, we can verify that our interpretation is correct by setting pE=pHp_{E}=p_{H}; in this case, ω⁡(k)→0,∀k\omega(k)\rightarrow 0,\,\forall k as PE=PH→1P_{E}=P_{H}\rightarrow 1, and the bias −δ​E[0]-\delta E^{[0]} disappears, as expected. Note that while this explains the upward bias at first order, the actual shape is, as we discussed, further distorted by shot noise, the fact that matrix elements do not actually have the same depolarization rate, and are themselves linear combinations of expectation values (see Eq. (II.3.2)), as well as the fact that there are multiple clusters in the NLCE sum.

IV Results

The simulations were programmed using qiskit [16], and the quantum experiments were performed on 5-8 qubits of an AQT Marmot 20-qubit trapped-ion quantum processing unit (QPU), with nominal single-qubit gate fidelity of 99.96%99.96\%, and two-qubit gate fidelities of 98.47%98.47\% [24], seated at the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre (LRZ) in Garching, Germany. We examined three systems: the one-dimensional TFIM, the TFIM chain in a longitudinal field (TFIM+LF), and the two-dimensional TFIM ladder.

For the cases involving a TFIM on a chain geometry, we performed one run for J/h=0.3J/h=0.3, two runs for J/h=0.8J/h=0.8 and three runs for J/h=1J/h=1, as well as three runs for TFIM+LF on a chain for J/h=0.5J/h=0.5 and hl=0.1h_{l}=0.1. For the TFIM on ladder, we performed a single run at J/h=0.2J/h=0.2. Each run comprised 2000 shots per matrix element, and as much for the ground state. The number of runs and shot budget were determined by the available QPU access time. See Tab. 1 for a summary.

For all cases combined, the total shot budget is about five million, which corresponds to around 430 hours of continuous runtime on the quantum device. Hence, due to the length of the calculations, which spanned several weeks, there is significant variability between the QPU runs. Despite this, the experimental dispersions generally adhere to the expectations, and more sampling could improve the stability of the results, as discussed in Sec. III. We compare our hardware (QPU) and noisy simulation results either to an analytic solution (available only for the TFIM in 1D) or to exact diagonalization (ED) within the NLCE framework, which we refer to as NLCE+ED. We additionally compare to statevector (SV) simulations, isolating the error introduced by VQE training from that of hardware noise.

IV.1 Model

The transverse-field Ising model (TFIM) is one of the paradigmatic models of the NISQ era, and a well-known test bench of quantum algorithms. The Hamiltonian for the TFIM in a longitudinal field is given by

H=−J∑⟨ν,μ⟩XνXμ−h∑νZν−hl∑νXν,H=-\,J\sum_{\langle\nu,\,\mu\rangle}X_{\nu}X_{\mu}-\,h\sum_{\nu}Z_{\nu}-h_{l}\sum_{\nu}X_{\nu}, (24)

where XX and ZZ are Pauli matrices, JJ denotes the Ising coupling for the nearest-neighbor spins, hh is the transverse field and hlh_{l} is the longitudinal field. In the absence of this longitudinal field (hl=0h_{l}=0), the TFIM exhibits ferromagnetic order for J>0J>0 and antiferromagnetic order for J<0J<0 on bipartite lattices, in the limit |J|≫h\left\lvert J\right\rvert\gg h. It possesses a global ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetry, corresponding to invariance under the simultaneous flip of all spins. The addition of the longitudinal field hlh_{l} breaks the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetry, thus leading to the mixing of the 0QP and 1QP states.

The model in Eq. (24) is symmetric under reflection, such that for an NN-qubit chain, HN−j,N−k=Hj,kH_{N-j,N-k}=H_{j,k}, and likewise for O~\tilde{O}. This also holds for the ladder geometry, which has a supplementary reflection symmetry about the centerline. Enforcing this symmetry allows us to effectively get twice the amount of shots per matrix element.

IV.2 Number of unique circuits

In Fig. 4, we show the number of unique circuits needed to compute an effective Hamiltonian of the TFIM model without longitudinal field for a one-dimensional chain and two-dimensional square lattice using the full NLCE+QA scheme, as a function of the number of qubits in the model.

By unique circuit, we mean that, given the same algorithm, two different non-commuting Pauli string measurements will require different basis changes at the end, resulting in two distinct circuits. For the TFIM, the total is computed as follows: one circuit is needed for the ground state, if it is measured using SQD; otherwise, a normal energy measurement is required, as explained thereafter. Each overlap measurement requires two circuits, one for the real part, and the other for the imaginary part. There are therefore 𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}) such circuits to compute for a given cluster CC. For the Hamiltonian matrix measurements, each Pauli string measurement that is off-diagonal requires four circuits, while diagonal ones are real and require only one. One can obtain an energy expectation of the one-dimensional TFIM with two circuits, one for the single ZZ terms, and one for the X​XXX terms. When adding a longitudinal field, we can use the XX-basis measurements. Finally, in order to perform the NLCE, multiple lattice sizes must be computed [14], and this depends both on the desired approximation level and dimensions. For a chain and a square lattice, the effective Hamiltonian for a single cluster of NN qubits requires

ncirc\displaystyle n_{\mathrm{circ}} =2​N2+2​(2​N2−N)+1\displaystyle=2N^{2}+2(2N^{2}-N)+1

circuits. This number of unique circuits grows polynomially with system size, which remains a tractable number. Each circuit is easy to compute on quantum devices, while the square lattice becomes potentially difficult for classical ones.

As mentioned in Sec. II.4, if we then add a longitudinal field, the overlap between the dressed ground state and its 1QP sector is non-vanishing, and we require 2​(2​N+1)2(2N+1) supplementary circuits.

For the NLCE calculation on the TFIM chain, we study the model for Nmax=5N_{\rm max}=5 on the quantum device, which requires two effective 1QP Hamiltonians on chain segments with 4 and 5 qubits need 230 unique circuits in total. The same NmaxN_{\rm max} for the TFIM chain with a longitudinal field requires 303 circuits. Finally, for the ladder TFIM, NLCE+QA with maximal cluster 4×24\times 2 needs 574 circuits.

IV.3 1QP dispersions

We look at the TFIM on a one-dimensional chain with hl=0h_{l}=0 in Eq. (24) which admits an exact solution via the Jordan-Wigner transformation [30]. Assuming h=1h=1, the 1QP dispersion ω⁡(k)\omega(k) at momentum kk is given by

ω⁡(k)=2​1+J2−2​J​cos⁡(k).\displaystyle\omega(k)=2\sqrt{1+J^{2}-2J\cos(k)}. (25)

The model undergoes a quantum phase transition at critical point Jc=1J_{c}=1, separating the quantum paramagnetic phase (J<1J<1) from the symmetry-broken ordered phase (J>1J>1). In this case, the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetry enforces vanishing overlap between the ground-state and the 1QP sector, so the PCAT reduces to the Schrieffer-Wolff transformation. For the 1D TFIM, the rectangular expansion used for NLCE, takes clusters of size 1×Ln≤Nmax1\times L_{n}\leq N_{\text{max}}. This simplifies NLCE for one-dimensional chain to a subtraction of two consecutive cluster sizes NmaxN_{\mathrm{max}} and Nmax−1N_{\mathrm{max}}-1, as contributions from smaller clusters cancel. The dispersion ω⁡(k)\omega(k) in the thermodynamic limit within NLCE taking into account clusters with up to NmaxN_{\mathrm{max}} sites, is therefore

ω⁡(k)\displaystyle\omega(k) =\displaystyle= ∑ν,μNmaxei​k​(ν−μ)​Heff,Nmax,ν,μ[1]\displaystyle\sum_{\nu,\mu}^{N_{\mathrm{max}}}e^{{\rm i}\,k\,(\nu-\mu)}H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},N_{\mathrm{max}},\nu,\mu} (26)
−\displaystyle- ∑ν′,μ′Nmax−1ei​k​(ν′−μ′)​Heff,Nmax−1,ν′​μ′[1],\displaystyle\sum_{\nu^{\prime},\mu^{\prime}}^{N_{\mathrm{max}}-1}e^{{\rm i}\,k\,(\nu^{\prime}-\mu^{\prime})}H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},N_{\mathrm{max}}-1,\nu^{\prime}\mu^{\prime}},

where Heff[1]H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff}} is obtained using Eq. (16).

Since the 1D TFIM admits an exact analytic solution, this case provides a direct benchmark for the hardware results. It is insightful to identify the performance of each part of the algorithm separately. The NLCE itself is an approximation truncated at the largest cluster size, introducing an error because spatial correlations from larger clusters are not considered. The quantum algorithm used will also not perfectly implement the adiabatic connection, whether a VQE or a finite-time sweep is used. The QPU’s depolarization noise will further distort the resulting dispersion relation, and the non-linear post-processing due to PCAT amplifies these errors. We investigate these sources of error by adding each layer of error in steps: first, the NLCE is computed with exact Hamiltonian matrices, then with a noiseless simulation of the quantum algorithm (leading to NLCE+QA), then with a noisy simulation, and finally on the QPU.

We now look at the NLCE+VQE setup described above to compute the dispersion in the thermodynamic limit. After the VQE is trained on classical resources, we compute all the required matrix elements on a QPU, and then perform PCAT and NLCE. Fig. 5 shows the results of noiseless, noisy, and QPU runs for the TFIM chain at J/h=0.3J/h=0.3. Right away, we notice that the noiseless dispersion overlays the analytic one, indicating that we should not expect error from the VQE being inaccurate. Secondly, the noisy simulation does not overlap with the analytic solution, for the reasons we discussed previously. It uses the reference depolarization rates, reproducing the behaviour in the second column of Fig. 3. Interestingly, the QPU dispersion in fact provides a better approximation than the noisy simulation would have suggested. Again, referring to Fig. 3, we see that the effective depolarization rate suggested by the QPU dispersion is closer to the third column in that figure, which may indicate that the reference depolarization rates overestimate the experimental ones. These dispersion curves were obtained with 2000 shots for each matrix element, corresponding to the second row of Fig. 3. Hence, we should expect that with more sampling, the QPU should model the dispersion very accurately.

We can error-mitigate the results by post-selecting the results. Since the preparation circuit for the TFIM without longitudinal field conserves the parity of the excitation number, we can conserve only odd parity outcomes. This would however reduce the shot count further and was therefore not performed. In fact, noisy simulations show that the net effect of loss in statistics due to post-selection actually increases the inaccuracy of the overall result.

Again using the conserved parity of the excitation number, we can also infer a depolarizing rate pOp_{O} from that symmetry, as discussed in Sec. III. Still, this results in further complications as the overall parity observable is global, so that its rate is different from that of the Hamiltonian terms [12]. Using more advanced techniques [7] would require an unacceptable sampling overhead, considering that the rate needs to be computed for each matrix element, meaning we must allocate a significant part of the shot budget to simply compute the depolarization rate. We have therefore not implemented it.

Now, in Fig. 6 we show an NLCE+ASP run on the QPU for the same model as discussed before, a pure TFIM chain at J/h=0.3J/h=0.3 in the thermodynamic limit with Nmax=5N_{\mathrm{max}}=5. Before we proceed, let us recall that the sweeping time need not be adiabatic with respect to single eigenlevels, but rather at an approximate subspace level, that is between the 1QP sector and the surrounding levels. Therefore, we have heuristically picked, for the results of Fig. 6, 10 time steps, each of which equal to 1/(|H0|+|H|)1/(\left\lvert H_{0}\right\rvert+\left\lvert H\right\rvert), with the total sweep time equal to the number of time steps, as described by An et al. [2]. We can see that this number of steps suffices to reproduce the dispersion relations in the noiseless case. In App. B we show simulations that motivate our choice.

Again, the noisy simulations are overestimating the depolarization rate in the device, and the QPU dispersion curve is closer to the analytic solution than the noisy simulation, indicating an actual depolarization rate closer, again, to the third column of Fig. 3. The ASP circuit, however, is 10 times deeper than the VQE circuit, causing a much higher noisy simulation dispersion curve, and a worse QPU result. We note that the QPU runs with higher J/hJ/h ratio adhere much closer to the noise model, as discussed in App. A.

Going closer to the quantum-critical point J/h=1J/h=1 for 1D TFIM, adding on a longitudinal field to it, or generally studying more complex models, the error rises as the norms of off-diagonal elements in the matrices grow. Fig. 7 displays the mean error of the dispersion curve with respect to the analytic solution (for pure TFIM), and for non-integrable models (TFIM on ladder and TFIM+LF on a chain), to the curve computed using exact diagonalization, as a function of the ratio J/hJ/h, while also including qualitatively different regimes, which are indicated by different colors. This graph presents a summary of multiple runs over multiple regimes, for which we show detailed presentations in App. A.

The pure TFIM chain is shown in green, and we recognize at J/h=0.3J/h=0.3 the curves shown in Figs. 5 and 6. The error grows as the value of J/hJ/h gets larger and moves closer to the critical point at J/h=1J/h=1. Because of the shallower circuit, the VQE almost always outperforms ASP except in a single case for J/h=0.8J/h=0.8. It is clear, however, that the mean error over multiple ASP runs should lie much higher than that for VQE runs, provided more data were available to compute a meaningful average. Indeed, we did not average the quantities in Fig. 7 because there are too few runs for the statistical mean to be properly representative of the true performance of different algorithms. Still, we note the fairly large difference between the different runs: this underlines the large variance in different realizations of the dispersion, which is due to the non-linear post-processing, as we discussed in Sec. III, and the fact that the data acquisition phase took place over a period of several weeks.

The orange crosses represent the error for the TFIM with a longitudinal field hl=0.1h_{l}=0.1 at J/h=0.5J/h=0.5 as discussed in Sec. IV.1; this field breaks the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetry, and the PCAT correction becomes fully utilized. Because the off-diagonal matrix elements are larger compared to the diagonal, the inversion is more sensitive, and the overall error larger.

We also consider the TFIM on a two-leg ladder at J/h=0.2J/h=0.2, the simplest two-dimensional geometry accessible with our cluster sizes. The ladder has a two-site unit cell, yielding two 1QP bands. Since the ladder is quasi one-dimensional, the rectangular NLCE expansion at Nmax=8N_{\mathrm{max}}=8 reduces to two consecutive cluster sizes, here 4×24\times 2 and 3×23\times 2, as in the chain case Eq. (26). We present detailed results for this model in App. A.4. In Fig. 7, the red crosses correspond to NLCE calculations for the TFIM ladder with the aforementioned cluster sizes. Despite the small value J/h=0.2J/h=0.2, the error is larger than the one of the TFIM chain for J/h=0.3J/h=0.3. This can be attributed to the larger qubit count and higher connectivity of the ladder geometry, and the fact that J/h=0.2J/h=0.2 is relatively closer to the ladder’s critical point J/h=0.545J/h=0.545 [44] than J/h=0.3J/h=0.3 is to the chain’s critical point J/h=1J/h=1.

V Conclusions

In this work, we explored the dispersion relations of transverse-field Ising models in the polarized phase using the NLCE+QA method, with expectation values computed on a 20-qubit AQT trapped-ion QPU. We introduced a simpler variant of the Hadamard test, the CX-test, which is particularly useful when computing a polynomial amount of matrix elements of a unitary in the computational basis. Using this test in combination with a specifically-trained VQE, we showed dispersion relations with better accuracy than the ASP, but we conjecture that decreasing error rates by a factor 1010 to 100100 should enable accurate computation of the dispersion relations with ASP. Using noisy simulations, we explored the effects of depolarizing noise on non-linear post-processing, to investigate the relationship between depolarization noise, shot noise, and their effect on the NLCE+QA framework.

While the computed dispersion does not always perfectly overlap the analytic dispersion, it can be made to approach it successfully for moderate Ising interactions in the polarized phase, sufficiently far from the quantum-critical point, showing that QPUs can generate data that is reliable enough for non-linear classical post-processing. Importantly, the PCAT construction guarantees cluster additivity of the final effective Hamiltonian on each cluster irrespective of the quantum algorithm used to prepare the input states. This means that different clusters within the NLCE expansion may be solved using different quantum algorithms, for instance VQE for some and ASP for others, while the resulting effective Hamiltonian remains cluster-additive by construction.

The full PCAT correction beyond the Schrieffer-Wolff transformation, which is relevant when the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetry of the TFIM is broken by the longitudinal field, could not be decisively tested at the current level of QPU precision. Errors in individual expectation values are already amplified through the non-linear processing inherent in the Schrieffer-Wolff transformation. As discussed in Sec. III, the correction Δi​j≪h/M\Delta_{ij}\ll h/\sqrt{M} is below the sampling-noise floor at the present shot budget. Demonstrating this correction would thus require more shots and lower hardware error rates.

As QPUs improve both in terms of noise rate and sampling rate, it may be possible to increase cluster sizes to obtain better approximations of the dispersion, and, eventually, compute the dispersion of models beyond classical means. We have shown in Fig. 4 that for a 10×1010\times 10 square lattice, the NLCE+QA procedure would require around 3⋅1063\cdot 10^{6} unique circuits, which at current QPU speeds, would require on the order of 10510^{5} hours of QPU time, underscoring the need for algorithmic improvements and faster sampling rates. Running multiple circuits in parallel on the quantum device is a straightforward improvement, and the reuse of some expectation values could further bring the number of circuits down.

Finally, determining how to mitigate error under the assumption of depolarizing noise seems to be a fruitful endeavor, and understanding the low-sampling edge cases when depolarizing noise can almost be assumed, but is not necessarily resolvable. Then, Pauli noise is not homogeneous and analysis becomes non-trivial.
